#3406. What’s It Like to Write Songs With Madonna, McCartney, and the Stones?

N o one has ever produced albums by both the Rolling Stones and Paul McCartney in the same year before, and those were just a couple of the highlights of Andrew Watt‘s last 12 months. Watt, who’s become music’s leading legend-whisperer, also continued his partnership with Lady Gaga on several new songs, worked on two tracks on Madonna‘s Confessions II, and produced Brandi Carlile’s Returning to Myself. His work with Michael Stipe on the soundtrack song “I Played the Fool’ led to an ongoing collaboration on Stipe’s upcoming solo album.

Watt talked about all of it and more in the latest episode of The Rolling Stone Studio. You can watch the whole conversation above, or read a lightly edited text version below.

Tell me about “Danceteria,” the song you-co-produced with Madonna, and the remix with Charli XCX.That song, in general, was just an amazing process to make. Talking with Madonna and hanging out with her, she has probably the coolest life of anyone. I’m from New York, so we just got into fun conversations about New York and, like, the scene and all the people that were around her. We started talking about Danceteria, which was the club where it all started for her.

As we were talking about the story of that place, it just became apparent that this should totally be a song. She would tell us, like, you look around and there’s Nile Rodgers and there’s David Byrne. And, like, all of the way that she was just talking about it seemed so cool, and she obviously invented talking on a pop song, right? And so it just felt so cool the way she was just naturally talking about it, so we threw the beat on, and then she started just talking about her life. It’s her origin story, and it’s amazing that it’s on a record, and you can listen to it whenever you want and hear all that. So I think Charli doing her [own] origin story was the cool thing for them being on it together.

I presume they did it separately. That’s how things go these days.Yeah, Charli recorded her part, but then they worked on the track and the production together, like, for a long time. We all kinda did, going back and forth. They’re both amazing producers. It’s a completely different record than the original. And I actually put them on a text message together to kinda meet and talk before they were ever gonna do a record together, because they just needed to be friends. They’re both so awesome and so cool, and really special people to me in my life. I was at a wedding with Charli, and I was like, “Have you ever met Madonna?” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

And she’s like, “No, we don’t know each other.” And so I thought that needed to happen. And then the song was just a natural progression.

What synergy did you see in their production styles as they worked together on it?Well, they’re both extremely detailed producers. Know exactly what they wanna hear, how something makes them feel. Very technical. Like, turn this up a dB or down, or it needs to be a bit bright, the EQ needs to change here, or the compression’s too strong, or we need a synth here that’s like this, maybe something more of a stab instead of a bass sound.

It’s very, very detailed. It’s so much fun to work with an artist who also is a producer because they know what they want. Sometimes you can be talking about production with anyone that you’re collaborating with, and you have to figure out what they mean in emotional terms, which is your job, you know?

Or, “It makes me feel like this,” or, “I want to feel like that,” and what does that correlate to musically? It’s so awesome when someone’s like, “Actually, it needs to do this,” and they just tell you straight up in technical terms. And the music’s always gonna come out better and, I think, more personal when the artist is also the producer. Related Content Mick Jagger Praises Sam Fender’s Rolling Stones Cover Historic Brian Jones Letter Inviting Charlie Watts to Join Rolling Stones in 1962 Surfaces The Birth of ‘Confessions II’: Producer Stuart Price Breaks Down Madonna's Instant Classic The Grammy for Producer of the Year, Non-Classical, Will Go to the Best Storyteller

In general, what surprised you about Madonna’s vibe in the studio?I just loved sitting with her and watching her writing process. She likes to work in small spaces, which I thought was really cool. Watching her process and how detailed she gets with her lyrics and how she’d go home and write and then bring in more the next day.

Probably my favorite part of working with her, there’s this song that we did on the album called “Lower East Side Girl,” and I was just sitting with a guitar, and Stuart [Price] and Cirkut and Madonna were there. It was the four of us. But we kind of went downstairs in the studio while the guys were focused a little bit on the track and the production, and we just sat there with a guitar, and I was playing it, and we were kind of singing it back and forth and just writing lyrics back and forth.

And she’s such an amazing songwriter. And sometimes people like to write their lyrics alone, and she did some of that as well, but writing with her in person and going back and forth and seeing how her mind works was really beautiful. I think it started a friendship between us.

I have a feeling there must have been way more songs with that group of collaborators than just those two songs.Well, we didn’t work for very long, which was what was cool. I think we had four days in the studio. And we made three songs in the four days, two of which came out. So that’s pretty good. I think we’ll definitely work together again. We’re text buddies now and talk about art and different things, and I just absolutely loved the process of working with her, and whenever she needs me, I’m there.

You obviously have the most insane list of phone contacts. Do you keep people under code names just in case?Some people get a middle name of Fucking. So Mick Jagger is not Mick Jagger. It’s Mick Fucking Jagger, right? That’s his name.

What was the worst one?I butt-dialed Keith Richards’ house once, and he does not like the phone. I got called back and you gotta, like, prep yourself to like be on the phone with Keith. It was just calling me back, and it was like, “Hello, you called me.” And it was just weird. It lasted only about, like, two seconds, which most phone calls with him last about 10 seconds, so.

Now, most people love working with you. Tony Iommi said that he didn’t want to make the final Black Sabbath album that you wanted to make because — strange reason — you were too excited about it.Yeah. That, I think is taken out of context. You know me. I’m definitely an excited musician, a person.

That part I bought.Yeah, that would be a true statement. But that’s not why it didn’t happen. Ozzy was wanting to continue to work and make stuff. And we were making music, and he had the idea, ’cause we were talking about, “Let’s try and do something a little different than…” The two albums that we made, Ordinary Man and Patient Number 9, were different albums, but they were of the same DNA.

So we’re like, “What could we do that’s different? Do you wanna make something with Tony? Should we make an Osbourne-Iommi album?” We were talking about that, and then he was just like, “Let’s make a Sabbath album.” He’s like, “We didn’t do an album with Bill Ward.” I think looking back at all the stuff he wanted to do, making an album with Bill was really important to him, and this was before Back to the Beginning was happening and everything. I think the idea of doing something with Bill was very, very important. And so one of the first incarnations of that was a potential album. As Ozzy does, [he] gave me the marching orders, “Call Tony. Then you call Geezer. Then you call Bill.” Right? So called Tony. “Would you wanna do it?” “Yeah, that sounds cool, if Bill would do it, yes.”

Geezer, “If Bill would do it, yes.” It was all about, “If Bill would do it, yes.” So then I had to have a conversation with Bill, and that was one of the strangest and funniest and coolest conversations. It was a long conversation. He was speaking in tongues.

Which, now knowing him and being friends with him, makes sense. Long story short, and without going into it too deeply, he was unable to do the album for personal reasons. And there was a nice, beautiful, long e-mail sent to all of us, and I was on an e-mail with the original members of Black Sabbath, which was pretty cool.

Then after we talked, it was like, “OK, Bill can’t do it, and there’s no reason to do it.” I’m sure Tony didn’t feel like going into all of that. Tony’s awesome. He’s a great friend to me. He’s a great mentor. We made a couple songs together on Ozzy’s album and had an amazing time working together.

I was definitely excited about the fact that it was going and everything, but that wasn’t the reason why we didn’t make the album.

Fair enough.I think he’s just taking the piss. Which anyone that wants to do that with me, they absolutely should.

I’ve heard there is some unreleased Ozzy stuff. Is there anything that you can say about that?There are some songs that we made for a specific reason. And yeah, that’s all I can say. They’re hard for me to listen to. I haven’t listened to them.

I’m sure. Any plans for them that you know of?Kind of. Back to the Beginning, the night before the concert, I actually went in Birmingham with Sharon and a couple of people to go get a curry, and I was texting with Ozzy, who was in his hotel room, and he was like, “Come to the hotel, come to the hotel.”

I was sitting with Sharon, and we were both like, “He has a big day tomorrow. Like, maybe I shouldn’t go ’cause he’ll get excited and everything.” But he was like, “No, you’re coming to the hotel. You are coming.” So I went, I brought a curry with me, and sat with him, and he was drawing like he usually does, and we sat and we listened to the stuff that we had made, and made notes.

And that and the next day were the last times I got to see him. But we had a beautiful listening session and talked about a lot of stuff. It’s hard to think about, but I miss him every day.

I love what he told you about bass in rock & roll.I take it with me all the time. It’s really true. He asked me, “What’s the loudest thing in a Led Zeppelin album?” I just said, John Bonham. Ozzy said it’s the bass: “The most important part in a rock & roll mix is the bass.” He had so many things he taught me about.

And if Ozzy Osbourne chose you, he gave you a career. I mean, he did it over and over and over again. I always loved rock music, but I was a pop producer before he chose to let me stand next to him and work with him, and then I got to do all these amazing things after. But he was the first one, and he chose Randy Rhoads. ‘Cause he chose Zakk Wylde, Jake E. Lee, and then even you get to, like, now currently, Yungblud.

Like, Yungblud was on an amazing path before the Back to the Beginning concert, but Ozzy chose “Changes” for him to sing and loved Dom as a person and what he was doing as an artist and brought him out there, and he sang that song, and it changed his life.

You made a great song with Michael Stipe, “I Played the Fool,” and now you’re working on his new album. How did you end up with Stipe in the first place?We met through Elton John. We actually went to go see a play that Elton had done the music for, and we sat next to each other. Talked as much as you can during an intermission where you’re watching a play. We also had to be extremely attentive — we were both sitting right next to Elton, so we’re listening to every piece.

I was scoring the show Rooster, which is made by Bill Lawrence and Matt Tarses. Bill is my future father-in-law. I’m engaged to his daughter, Charlotte. And so we wanted to do something fun together, so I thought, “I’ll score one of your shows,” and this one really made sense, and it’s based around Steve Carell, and his character is a writer who comes to a college campus to kinda save his daughter, who’s going through some stuff, so he takes a guest-in-residence job. The sound of the show kinda became the musical sounds of bands that Steve, his character, Rooster, would’ve been listening to when he went to college — because he doesn’t go for this reason, but he ends up reliving his college experience.

When we were talking about the great Eighties American college bands, R.E.M. was the first one that came up, and both Bill and Matt’s favorite band is R.E.M., so there was a personal thing involved as well. So when that started happening, I was like, “I actually just met Michael this year, and so let me see if I can get in touch with him.”

So I asked Elton to put us in touch, and Michael says he answered because Elton’s never gave his phone number to anyone else ever. And so we met and hit it off and started working on this thing. And yeah, he’s become an awesome friend. I’m gonna see him later today, actually.

Michael has been working on a solo album for a really long time. It seems like he hasn’t wanted to get to the finish line. What is your sense of that?I don’t think that’s the case. He, as all great artists are, he’s extremely hard on himself. He works really hard at his craft, and he kinda beats himself up, I think, in a healthy way.

I’ve seen him write lyrics, throw them out, write them again, do all his own merit, you know? So I think he is wanting to make sure that he is gonna say exactly what he wants to say, and make a sound that’s exactly how he wants it to sound.

One of the things that he said is that he really misses — with R.E.M., they wrote beds of music, and he sang over them. So I think part of the challenge is to figure out what can substitute for that.Yeah, the key is he’s working with a bunch of different people, so… And it’s exactly that. Different flavors of different beds, and then finding his way around them, but he’s one of the all-time greats, great songwriter, great lyricist, great melodist. And really fun to be around.

The McCartney album is very adventurous in a lot of its choices. It’s very produced. In addition to some tight folky songs, there’s some great Wings-like guitar excursions, really letting him go out there. How much of that was his idea, and how much was you nudging him a little bit?Well, what was really cool about that record is it was just the two of us. Like, the whole time. So we’d just be bouncing off of each other. He is a hundred-percenter, which there are very few of. Can play every instrument, can mix, can produce, write every word, write every melody. Write all the chords. I mean, he does 100 percent of it.

His choice to have a producer is not out of necessity. It’s out of desire. So he likes to bounce off someone sometimes. I got the incredible honor of taking that role this time around. We would just have fun in the studio. Sometimes things would start from nowhere, which is not a common thing for him.

The way the Beatles would work, they would have songs that they’d write. They’d go over them at Paul’s place, which is around the corner from the studio, Abbey Road, and have a coffee and a cigarette in Paul’s garden, go over the songs, go over to the studio. There’d be one session in the morning for however long it was.

They’d take a break, and then they’d do the other session. I think they’re two, three-hour blocks or whatever. They’d take them both. They’d record two songs a day, and that’s how the Beatles made their music. His process is not, “Let’s go into the studio with nothing and see what happens” a lot.

And we got to do that here a little bit. So that’s how we ended up actually writing a couple of things together ’cause the guitars would come out, and we’d get on a thing. We’d get on a tangent and follow it down. There was never a point until, like, the last, like, two or three months in the five years that we spent working together where we were like, “OK, we’re making an album.”

It would just be like, “Hey, Andrew, I’m coming to L.A. at this time. Do you have a couple weeks to just kinda mess around?” And that’s what we would do. And we’d collect songs, and then we started working on some of the things that he had already started and everything, and then it kinda just turned into this natural, natural thing.

But working with him is like going to college. You know? Every time I’d get those couple weeks with him, I’d be a better musician, a better producer. I’d have more chord knowledge. Right after you work with Paul, you’re like, “OK, I’m ready to get right back in the studio” because, like, you’re better. You know? And then that eventually goes away because you’re not spending as much time with him.

When you have that incredibly rare privilege of sitting across from Paul McCartney and making a song from scratch, what do you learn about the essence of his creativity?His process is amazing. Him being around a collaborator is cool. His time alone is extremely important. Tucking away, often in a small space and writing, taking stuff home and writing in the morning. He’s fearless. And our whole collaboration started from, we were having tea. We were introduced by his manager, and he went to tell me, “You know, you can write a song out of anything.”

And he went to go grab a guitar. He’s like, “Oh, you only have righty guitars.” And I actually had some lefties brought over….

Just in case, right?Yeah. I woke up in a sweat the night before thinking, “What if he wants a guitar? What’s gonna happen?” I didn’t have any lefties. So—

But see, this is part of why you’re where you are, because you thought of that.I thought of it at the last second. Barely thought of it. Gave him a lefty. He played this weird chord, and then he’s kind of giggling to himself in a boyish way. It was such a weird chord that he had to resolve it. And once he resolved the chord, it was time to go to a third chord, and then the guitars came out, and we kind of—

And that’s the opening track of the album.That’s the opening track of the album. “As You Lie There.” And so that song was so much fun. Once that was there, it was kind of like, OK, let’s use the studio in all these fun ways, and he was kind of, like, teaching me the way he works. That was the point. It was like, you can write a song out of anything, and then sometimes you switch it up and go to a weird thing. It changes form a million different times, that song. And then it goes to a rock section. Then it goes to a bluesy guitar section. You know? It was kind of like, let me show you how we can use the studio. That’s how that song kinda came together.

And all of a sudden you realize why he’s the guy who made “Uncle Albert” and the Abbey Road medley and all this stuff.He loves playing characters, even, like, “Rocky Raccoon.” Who’s that guy? You know? He loves to play different characters and do voices, and his imagination is unlike anyone else’s. Like Mozart, you know? Bouncing around the studio and playing every different instrument, watching him do that, watching him know to play the cymbals quieter than the snare drum.

I asked him why he did that. He’s like, “So that you could crank the overheads, and it’s gonna sound great, and you’re not gonna be, you know, bashing people in the head with cymbals.” He’s thinking about all that stuff. Watching him arrange background vocals, which he does either at the piano or with a guitar in his hand at the mic, and goes through the note and sings it, and is really choosing the notes and arranging them.

He’s incredible at coming up with the perfect part on every different instrument and not making you feel like he played any instrument worse than the other. I mean, it just sounds like someone who’s a master on each instrument. Sounds like a band.

The Stones album is also incredible, in a very different way. Paul is kind of addressing mortality and looking back, whereas Mick and Keith and Ron sound immortal — libidinous and alive, as if they’re gonna go on forever. How do you even make sense of the amount of energy they bring?It’s a trippy thing to think about, right? Because for us, rock & roll’s been in our life forever, but in the history of music, it’s not that old of a genre. The Stones guys, they wanna rock. That’s what they wanna do. They want it to be loud, and get in the studio, and have drums, and push the tempos. And as with all bands that we love, it’s not about one person.

It’s the sum of all parts. You can listen to a Keith Richards solo album, they’re awesome. You listen to Mick’s solo albums, they’re awesome. Or Ronnie’s solo albums, there’s songs on there I love. When those three guys play together, the roof leaves the building.

It’s something that doesn’t sound like anything else in how they interpret each other and how they play off of each other. When I made those records, I would always be in the live room while the band tracked, kind of as far from Keith as I am from you, and Mick kinda right in front, and be in that circle so I could watch how they’re interplaying with each other and what they’re doing.

It helped me so much to understand, like, the chords and what they’re playing, and to be able to help arrange things as they were happening. And you don’t want it to ever be an arduous process with a band like that. They’re magic. If you’ve seen a Stones show, you see what happens when they hit a magic moment. It’s like, you wanna be able to help that happen as quick as possible when they’re playing a song. So my job would be to have a mic like this and call sections. “B section.” That one’s—

The conductor.Yeah, try and not get [my voice] into the overheads too much, and like, they kinda look up and switch, you know?

And, “OK, let’s go back to the A section. Take it out on that,” you know? And like, to make codas and stuff like that. So it would just be kind of, they’re playing the tune that they made and I’m arranging it as it’s happening in the moment.

Kind of amazing. If you had to guess, will there be another Stones album?I don’t know. I don’t know. I didn’t know if there was gonna be another one after the first one. If they call, I’m there. It’s the greatest honor of my life being around that band.

You’ve worked with so many great people, so many of your heroes. Where does that leave you as far as goals?I don’t ever really think like that. I’ve been so blessed to meet all these amazing people, and that turns into us working together. The artists that I’ve worked with has been a natural progression of meeting them and it making sense for us to work together. So I’m never really, like, going after someone or something like that. Things come into my life, and then I think about how amazing it would be to work with that person. But yeah, my antenna is open as always.

I think a lot of what you do is cross-pollinate. You’re bringing things from pop into rock, and vice versa, into K-pop, into whatever. You’re planting seeds, bringing sounds and people together. That seems like your overall thing.Yeah. I will say this, pop music is in a great place right now. You’re seeing the rise of all of these amazing pop girls coming back. It’s always been a big part of mainstream music, but there’s a lot of new artists breaking, and so that’s really exciting to me, too. I’ve been having fun making some pop music again, which I’m always doing as I’m making rock records as well. A part of the fun of my job is to get to work in all these different genres, but I’m really excited about what I’m hearing in pop music right now.

Your collaboration with Gaga is obviously ongoing. You did “The Dead Dance,” you did all those songs for The Devil Wears Prada 2. Tell me about those ongoing sessions. What’s it like to go back with her?Greatest feeling in the world is, like, when you make a project with an artist, it ends, and everyone’s sad, and you’re gonna miss each other, and then they call you back, and they’re like, “Let’s make more stuff.” You feel so great about yourself because that means they enjoyed working with you, they enjoyed the process.

She and I are from the same place. We’re from New York. We both grew up playing in the Bitter End, and were walking in the same streets, and in the same scenes a couple years apart. And so our foundation of music and our references are very aligned. So it feels like my sister, you know? Like my older sister, couple years older than me. When we sit, we break a song down, even when it’s an electronic song, and I’m on the guitar and she’s on the piano, sitting head-to-head and going through the song, it’s one of the most beautiful experiences of my life. It’s brought me to tears multiple times. It’s awesome.

Do you have a sense of when you’re working with her again?No. We’re in touch all the time, and it’s the same kinda thing. Whenever she sounds the bell, I’ll be there.

How do you work out the priority thing? What if Mick and Paul and Gaga all want you on the same day? What the hell do you do?It’s happened. You hold on, you breathe, and you figure out a way to make it all work. I find that if you are transparent always — it’s a big thing for me, transparency, especially in the music business. There’s so many people that are not that way.

And honest. You’re not lying to them.Yeah, that’s what I mean. People seem to react to that, and will follow you, and they’ll tell you when they really need you. And other people will be like, “Yeah, it’s OK. Well, let’s do it tomorrow,” whatever, you know? Or then there’s sometimes when everyone wants you at the same time, and then it gets fucked. But there’s always a way through it if you’re transparent and honest and real.

We were talking about cross-pollinating. What do you see in these veteran rock stars, and what do you see in the young pop stars you work with? What are the chief things you think they can learn from each other?They’re all different. And everyone works differently. And so you take something from that project, then you bring it into your next project. It’s just, like, natural. A great example of that for me was when I was working on the first Stones album, I had, like, a week off, and then we started the Pearl Jam album. And Keith had just showed me how to play in open G tuning and, like, gave me basically lessons and was like, “This is how you do it.” Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Appeals Court Says Lawsuit Over ‘The Pitt’ Can Proceed, Cites ‘Numerous’ Similarities to ‘ER’ As Nicki Minaj Rallied for Trump's GOP, Her Lawyers Told Court She Still Owes Them $295,000 Bob Dylan Meets With Pope Leo XIV in a Private Audience

And I started writing like that in my own way. And then he was, like, laughing. He was like, “You’re off to the races,” you know? And then I was able to take being able to play like that into Pearl Jam, and then there’s a song on the album that ended up in open G called “Wreckage,” that was directly influenced from learning open G tuning from the Stones.

And then that was just, like, a cool thing, you know? Learning how to record bands and capturing live energy is something that I try to bring into the pop music that I make. And the idea of performance-based music all the way through, not flying loops. That’s great, too. I do that all the time. Love doing that, but music that’s performed top-down does a different thing to you. So I try to incorporate that into the pop music and electronic music that I make as well.

Andrew Watt talks about working with the world’s biggest artists in an episode of The Rolling Stone Studio

#3404. Adam Driver Says No More Kylo Ren: ‘Star Wars’ “Ship Has Sailed”

We know Adam Driver has no plans to return to Lena Dunham’s Girls reboot, but what about the Star Wars franchise? Any chance fans will see Kylo Ren again?

“Yeah, yeah, it’s over,” Driver said this week on The Rich Eisen Show podcast with regard to the possibility that he’d return to play Kylo Ren. “No more Star Wars. We tried. We tried to do one more, but they were like, no, he’s dead.”

The character was killed off in The Rise of Skywalker (2019), although Driver says on the podcast that she and Steven Soderbergh had indeed worked on a standalone Kylo Ren movie that never came to fruition. Watch on Deadline

“We got a script together that was really good with Scott Burns and Rebecca Blunt,” Driver tells Eisen about the standalone project that had the working title The Hunt for Ben Solo. “We all worked on it. It was awesome. It was really cool.”

“They didn’t see how Ben Solo was alive,” he said. “And that was that.”

Driver points out that ultimately the decision of whether or not to bring back the character isn’t his to make. “If they wanted to, fine, but it’s not our call,” the actor said. “I think the ship has sailed, though.”

Driver is currently starring in James Gray’s Paper Tiger along with Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller. Set in 1986 Queens, NY, the film follows two brothers who become entangled in a scheme that ends up involving the Russian mafia. The film premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May, and is being released November 13 by Neon.

#3403. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3401. Report: Apple and Samsung outperform rivals as smartphone chip shipments tumble 21%

According to Counterpoint Research, Apple and Samsung were the only major smartphone chip vendors to gain market share in Q3 2026, as global shipments declined 21% year-over-year. Here are the details.

At this point, most 9to5Mac readers are probably familiar with the challenges that smartphone vendors have been facing due to rising memory costs, and how Apple has managed to weather the impact better than many of its competitors.

Over the past few months, many reports have noted that while most smartphone vendors raised prices more than once throughout the year, Apple held off on increasing iPhone prices until September, with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series.

Those same reports have been showing the iPhone outperforming the broader market in smartphone, even as the industry experiences a sharp downturn.

That said, Counterpoint Research recently published a report (via MacMagazine) examining how rising memory costs and slowing smartphone demand have affected the global smartphone chip market.

According to the report, Apple remained in third place among smartphone chip vendors in the third quarter, with its market share increasing from 17% in Q3 2025 to 21%.

MediaTek still led the global smartphone SoC market with a 28% share (down 6 percentage points year-over-year), followed by Qualcomm with 22% (down from 25%).

After Apple, UNISOC ranked fourth with 13% (down from 14%), while Samsung remained in fifth with an 8% share, up from 6% in Q3 2025. Other manufacturers went from a 4% share to 8%.

Overall, the market saw a 21% decline year-over-year, though the report didn’t disclose how many chips were shipped during the quarter.

Commenting on the numbers, Counterpoint Research Senior Analyst Shivani Parashar said:

“We saw three notable flagship chipset launches in September 2026, based on TSMC’s 2nm process node: Apple’s A20 series, MediaTek’s Dimensity 9600 Pro and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 series. These launches are expected to boost premium smartphone SoC shipments in Q4 2026, although volumes are still likely to remain below Q4 2025 levels.”

Looking ahead, Counterpoint expects global smartphone chip shipments to decline 20% year-over-year in 2026, followed by another 3% to 4% drop in 2027. The research firm also expects memory prices to continue rising next year.

During its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, Apple described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” warning that further increases would continue to put pressure on its profit margins in the coming quarters.

To read Counterpoint’s full report, follow this link.

#3400. Meet the Vigodas: Conan O’Brien Plays Out His Teenage Dream With L.A. Cover Band

When Conan O’Brien takes the stage at the Teragram Ballroom in downtown Los Angeles on Friday night, he’s wearing tight black jeans, a custom black jacket sporting the band’s name, and a wide smile. He greets the crowd by asking how many people had seen his cover band, the Vigodas. A few shout that they had, but the vast majority were there to see him for the first time. And despite his fame, that makes sense. Though he’s probably one of the most recognizable and beloved people in Hollywood, at this point, the band has only done about 10 shows around Southern California since premiering in August.

They draw a wide range of fans. Some know him from his days hosting Late Night, while others seem to be dedicated listeners to his long-running interview podcast, Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend —a smattering appear young enough to have only seen clips of him during his network heyday. The band run through more than a dozen covers — from Elvis Presley and Elvis Costello to Bo Diddley and John Lennon — an eclectic mix of rock & roll spanning the 1950s through the 1980s that is probably best described as the music that won’t get out of O’Brien’s head.

“When I was in college, when everyone else was starting to listen to U2 and Oingo Boingo, I was into hardcore rockabilly,” O’Brien, 63, tells Rolling Stone backstage before the show, running his fingers through the front of his ginger mane, which leaves it in a four-inch wave above his head. “I had the hair for it.” He loved the raucous sounds of Jerry Lee Lewis and early Elvis Presley. “Over the years, I would pick up these songs that were like adrenaline,” he says. “One of them is Ronnie Hawkins’ version of ‘40 Days,’” which they play later during their set.

Though the crowd never seems to break a sweat, they’re engaged through the hour-plus set, occasionally singing along and doing little solo swing dances in place. (There are also a surprising number of couples making out.) But the best part of the night is the overwhelming joy on O’Brien’s face as he jams onstage with four other guys 20 years his junior, whom he only met a few months ago but became fast friends.  Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

O’Brien is probably still best known for his decades as a talk-show host, but it was the podcast that launched the band, he says, when he had singer Norah Jones on in May 2023. “I’ve known Norah over the years, and she always remembered me having a guitar whenever she would come do the late-night show,” O’Brien says. “She said, ‘How’s the guitar going?’ And I said, ‘You know, it’s kind of sad because I don’t really have anyone to play with, and I need someone to kind of kick my ass and help my game.’ She said, ‘I know a guy.’”

The guy was guitarist Jason Roberts, who’d played in Jones’ band for half a decade. He started giving O’Brien lessons, and they would nerd out about their shared love of the Beatles. “We text about the Beatles a lot,” Roberts says later. “We just both love the Beatles so much.”

About six months ago, O’Brien asked Roberts if he’d be down to take their lessons to the next level. “He was just like, ‘Can you help me put a band together?’” Roberts remembers. “And I said, “I know the exact guys for this.” O’Brien tells the same story. “A week later, we’re in Hollywood, and we’re playing,” he says. “I’m just floating, so happy.”

They named themselves after the late actor Abe Vigoda — another towering figure with an expressive face, best known for his roles in The Godfather and Barney Miller. “Abe was a fixture on my old late show, he did hundreds of bits for us, and he was a sweet and hilarious man. I always knew his iconic mug was the face of our band,” says O’Brien. He had never played in a band as a teenager, but always wanted to. “For years and years and years, you could argue that the only reason I wanted a late-night show was so I could have a band,” he says. Back when he was working with the Max Weinberg 7, and later Jimmy Vivino and the Basic Cable Band, he would join them to jam every time they had rehearsal. “I’d put on a guitar and I would play with them and sing songs,” he says. “We had a good repertoire. And then when I went through my Tonight Show madness” — referring to the six months he spent behind the desk of the NBC institution from 2009 to 2010 — “we went out on the road and we did a comedy show, but also it had a lot of music in it too, and that was my happy place.”  Related Content Jack White, Barack Obama, Conan O’Brien Celebrate Stephen Colbert as ‘The Late Show’ Ends Conan O’Brien to Bring His Irreverent Comedy to the Oscars for Third Consecutive Year Jimmy Kimmel Forms Cover Band With Conan O’Brien, Jon Stewart at Netflix Is a Joke Fest Oscars Boss Reveals What You Didn’t See on TV: ‘Sinners’ Performance Ran Long, Speech Snafus, More

O’Brien seems comfortable as a cover man, satisfied to reinterpret the music he loves — often by speeding them up. A few years ago, he ran into Beverly D’Angelo at a party, and she commented to him at just how fast his version of “40 Days” was when she heard it on tour. Earlier this year, when the Rolling Stones asked him to introduce them and their new album at a concert in Brooklyn, he ran into Keith Richards backstage. “Keith said to me, he said, ‘I heard your ‘Monkey Business,’” O’Brien says, referring to the Chuck Berry cover he recorded with Jack White for 2010’s Live at Third Man. O’Brien was surprised he knew who he was, much less had heard his 16-year-old record. “You’re kidding,” he replied. “[Keith] went, ‘You sound like a fucking auctioneer.’” O’Brien laughs. “He’s not wrong.”

Part of the joy of the band is the excuse to tour different venues in Los Angeles. Their first show was at Permanent Records Roadhouse, a tiny club in East L.A. where they played as a surprise guest after Fred Armison’s regularly scheduled set. Since then, they’ve had a tour of Los Angeles’ finest small stages, from the Troubadour to the Lodge Room to the Moroccan Lounge. “I’m a connoisseur of kooky backstages,” he says, remembering a time he hung out with his friend and idol Bob Newhart backstage at the Chicago Theatre. “I had a goofy dressing room, and Bob Newhart said, ‘Conan, no matter what you achieve in show business, whenever you get to the theater and they show you your dressing room, there’s always a piece of dead brown lettuce on the floor. That’s just the way it is.” He smiles at the thought. “It’s very humbling.” Trending Stories A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope Richard Lloyd, Television's Virtuoso Guitarist, Dead at 75 Houston Mayor Limits Cooperation With ICE: ‘Elections Matter’ Good Riddance to the Cybertruck, the Chariot of the Dumbest Gods

Aside from getting to see the bowels of these Art Deco monuments, the other point of the band, O’Brien says, is to be able to share the stage with other musicians whose work he loves. There are the folks in his outfit, sure — Roberts the guitarist, Erik Kertes on bass, Ben Alleman on keys, and Josh Adams on drums (Rob Jensen filled in on Friday for Adams, who is on tour with the Fruit Bats). But there are all the openers, too, like Malena Cadiz tonight — an Americana singer-songwriter with a lush voice — or Sam Evian, who opened for them at Pappy and Harriet’s out in Joshua Tree a few weeks ago. Each night, he asks those openers to join them for a song or two. “I want it to be a hootenanny,” O’Brien says. “I want it to be something where we roll along and other people jump in. Because I have no future in the music business, but I can be like a small part of it.”

#3399. What to Expect From Best Buy's Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales This Year

For all intents and purposes, Black Friday sales are already here. There are plenty of deals out already, even though we're weeks away from the actual event. Best Buy has announced the following events:

DoorBoosters: A Halloween sale from Oct. 30 to Nov. 1.

Early Black Friday Deals and Doorbusters: The official start of early Black Friday deals on Nov. 6. New deals will drop every Friday.

Black Friday Doorbusters and Deals: Best Buy says this will be its main sale, starting on Thursday, Nov. 19 and running until Nov. 28 with deals on "computing, gaming, home theater, wearables, and more."

Cyber Sunday and Monday: Best Buy is extending Cyber Monday to five days and says you can find deals going up to 50% off select tech.

You can find deals on TVs, laptops, headphones, video games, electric bikes, and more. #3398. Apple now lets developers offer discounts when users move to cancel subscriptions

Apple today rolled out a new subscription retention tool for developers looking to reduce cancellations. Here are the details.

During WWDC earlier this year, Apple announced Retention Messaging, a new feature that lets developers display personalized messages and special offers to users as they attempt to cancel their subscriptions.

Now, as the company explained in a new post on its developer blog, the feature is available, allowing developers to configure messages that “appear in the cancellation flow and can include text, images, or a special offer.”

If this sounds familiar, that’s because this is not Apple’s first attempt to help developers reduce cancellations.

Here’s Apple on how developers can configure these messages:

Apple’s documentation notes that developers can create up to 10 retention messages per app, each associated with one or more subscriptions.

With October in the can, we can finally say goodbye to the Sunday scaries. Hoorah! Now that Netflix’s November 2026 schedule is set, we’ve got plenty of great new content to get stuck into. This week, I’ve gone for a trio of shows that contain mercifully few frights.

First up is the highly-anticipated second season of “Black Doves”, where Keira Knightley continues to shine as the wife of the British Prime Minister… oh, and she’s also a covert spy. Next is the debut of “Will Trent” on Netflix. If you’ve slept on this charming detective drama, you’ve got a whole lot of binge-watching ahead of you this weekend with all four seasons now available. Lastly, season two of “North of North” is streaming, and Siaja’s chilly Canadian misadventures continue to delight.

Whether you're pining for spy thrills or gentle laughs with a detective and his tiny pooch, here are three fresh Netflix releases you should definitely add to your weekend watchlist.

Talk about the best of British. “Black Doves” season 2 rocks an absolutely stellar cast of Blighty greats. Keira Knightley continues to impress as a covert agent who keeps leaking national secrets for the titular spy agency. Naughty Keira! She’s reunited with her handler Mrs. Reed (a typically charismatic Sarah Lancashire), who promptly goes missing, driving much of this season’s plot.

Our secrets-sharing protagonist also gets reacquainted with her best pal Sam (Ben Whishaw), who just so happens to be a professional assassin… and a bit of a drunk. This high-tension drama also benefits from the arrival of “Scream” legend Neve Campbell. Well plotted and stylishly shot, you can tell the Big N has chucked a huge amount at this thriller.

Watch "Black Doves" season 2 on Netflix now

The first four seasons of this detective drama are now available to stream on Netflix, and "Will Trent" really does feel like a love letter to “Monk”. Tipping its hat to Tony Shalhoub’s awkward but brilliant homicide cop, the titular star of this show (played by Ramón Rodríguez) also struggles in social situations due to his dyslexia. Yet there’s no other agent you’d want on your case if you suddenly found your corpse ditched down a drainpipe.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Much of the action of “Will Trent” focuses on whether our hero can Sherlock his way through various Atlanta-based crimes. But the real hook beyond your standard police procedural tropes? That would be Will’s relationship with a newly adopted chihuahua called Bluebell. This easy going show has serious “Turner & Hooch” vibes. I’m all in.

Watch "Will Trent" seasons 1-4 on Netflix now

Talk about a perfect show for these dark winter months. Focused on Ice Cove, Nunavut, this breezy comedy is set in Canada’s northernmost territory, meaning there’s a whole lot of daylight action. We’re once again back with Siaja (Anna Lambe), a young mother who’s still trying to figure out life post-divorce. In this second season, romance is back on the table, as our Inuk heroine enters the icy pools of the speed dating scene.

A big part of the show focuses on community, and Siaja now has to deal with new job demands under her boss Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub, who you might remember as the irrepressible Chloe from “24”). “North of North” doesn’t trade in Jack Bauer breakneck action, but the show’s gentle laughs are occasionally punctuated with low-stakes drama, like a mini water crisis. Easy giggles and gorgeous scenery. What’s not to like?

Watch "North of North" season 2 on Netflix now

#3395. Zohran Mamdani and Puerto Rican Band Chuwi Discuss Gentrification, Music, and Making Change

The Puerto Rican band Chuwi, made up of siblings Lorén, Willy, and Wester and their best friend Adrián, has spent the last couple years achieving international fame through a major collab with Bad Bunny, also ending up as his opening act on tour. But they’ve also used their platform to speak out about Puerto Rico — their debut album, Libertad, from last month, tackles government corruption, the economic and social effects of colonialist policies, and more — and on Friday, they joined Mayor Zohran Mamdani in San Juan for a conversation about issues central to the islands’ future.

As part of a visit engaging local organizations and community leaders, Mamdani sat down with the musicians to hear more about their perspective. “I look forward to listening to Puerto Ricans to hear about what the struggles are that they’re facing and how New York City can be a partner in fighting for working people wherever they may call home,” the mayor told Rolling Stone.

The meeting was part of the annual Somos Conference, where New York State lawmakers meet with Latino advocates over four days in Puerto Rico. The conference’s goal is to create a space where attendees can speak directly with those in positions of power about what’s most important to their communities.

This year marks the 40th anniversary of the event, and it is customary for the mayor of New York City to attend. Last year, Mamdani flew down just days after he was elected. This year, he returned, 10 months into his first term, and seemed clear-eyed about what he wanted to talk about during his 72 hours in town. His central focus is bridging the gap between the archipelago and the nearly 600,000 Puerto Ricans who call New York City home, with Mayor Mamdani targeting issues that matter to both.

“What I’ve heard from Puerto Rican New Yorkers is a concern about displacement and gentrification, not only in the neighborhoods that they’ve helped to build in New York City, but also right here in Puerto Rico,” he says.The mayor met with various coalitions and activist groups, such as Defend Cabo Rojo, FURIA, La Tejedora, and PR No Se Vende (“Puerto Rico Is Not for Sale”) that have dedicated themselves to combatting those challenges. But before those meetings, he scheduled an equally important sit-down with Chuwi, given their mission to spread the word about Puerto Rico’s struggles through their music. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Chuwi became a household name after they collaborated on the song “WELTiTA” off Bad Bunny’s Grammy-winning DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS. They went on to be the opening act of his 59-date world tour. On Libertad, the band went back to their protest music roots and leaned more than ever into the politics. They’ve addressed some of these themes on the album since their earliest EPs, but never as directly as the LP.

Lorén initiated the conversation with Mamdani by describing how she was in New York City the week before the 2025 election. She told him she was impressed by the enthusiasm she saw for his campaign, saying that she found it very inspiring as a Puerto Rican. “What you guys are doing is inspiring,” Mamdani said, complimenting how they use their music to spread important messages without compromising the artistic side.

“When you’re not at a desk, it’s easier to tell the truth,” he said. He noted that as artists, they have the unique privilege of being able to speak out and that their music is a connection to home for many fans. Indeed, even Bad Bunny himself said last year that listening to Chuwi during his time living in Los Angeles pre-DtMF made him homesick.

Willy took the opportunity to ask Mayor Mamdani about how he’s been able to achieve so much in his term so far: “Why is it you can do these policies that other mayors couldn’t?” Related Content Puerto Rico’s Next Big Music Movement Is Pop Introducing Rolling Stone’s National Affairs Newsletter  Chuwi’s Debut Album ‘Libertad’ Is As Powerful As It Is Catchy Mayor Mamdani and Nas Have a Heart to Heart About Keeping NYC the Home of Hip Hop

“When you get elected you get disconnected,” Mamdani said. He explained that leaders can become cut off from the people they serve, and that the environment can turn into tinted SUVs and private hotel rooms. He gave examples of things he does “intentionally” to stay connected, like biking around the city. “Institutions change slower than people,” and too much patience sometimes inadvertently leads to complacency. “The more you stay with the people the more you stay impatient. You have to keep [them] around you,” he says.

Chuwi pointed out how skeptical many citizens are about politicians, and how cynicism has become the prevalent feeling, especially in a Puerto Rico that has been suffering economically for almost two decades, even before Hurricane María dealt a blow to its infrastructure in 2017.

Mamdani acknowledged that feeling, and said Puerto Ricans might be skeptical because “they know about history.” He said he’s aware of the gap between what politicians promise and what citizens actually expect them to deliver on. “How do you collapse that separation?” he said, sharing that he feels “inspiration” is a stronger force than “disillusionment” and that he tries to wake up every day “ready to fight” and to “use pressure in a productive way.”

Aware of how heated things can get in politics, and having been on the receiving end of a fair share of criticism, Willy asked how the mayor deals with mud-slinging and negative rhetoric in politics. Mamdani said that treating people who disagree with him harshly or with judgment leads to both sides feeling like there has to be a winner or loser in the debate. He stressed the importance of speaking to people who aren’t just “those who feel comfortable with you.”

Mamdani then pivoted to asking Chuwi about their future plans. The band said that they’ll be returning to cities they visited over the summer, hinting at a big tour of their own. Mamdani playfully reminded them he used to be an artist as well — as an indie rapper going by the alias Mr. Cardamom — and reminisced about how rough it was the first few years. “I was the opener to the opener to the opener,” he joked. “I once performed at 5 p.m. for a band that was playing at 9 p.m. I was singing to the seat savers.”He said he was delighted by the possibility of Chuwi going to different countries with their music, because as he put it, “through that, others will hear and see their own struggles.”

Lorén thanked the mayor for meeting with them, sharing that their grandparents were one of the families that moved to New York City during the post-WWII migration wave, and in fact got married in the city. Mamdani stressed the importance of Puerto Ricans in the history of New York, especially in organized labor movements. Lorén shared that her grandfather worked at a textile factory in the city.

Willy capped off the meeting by thanking Mayor Mamdani for meeting with the organizations working on the ground in P.R. He stressed how important their goals were when it came to pushing for the abolition of Puerto Rico’s tax haven status, protecting the coastal maritime-terrestrial zone, and trying to stop large developments that threaten Puerto Rico’s habitats like Esencia in Cabo Rojo and Moncayo in Fajardo, among other causes. “Politicians [in Puerto Rico] won’t meet with them unless it’s in a court room or public hearings,” he said. Trending Stories A Jesuit Priest Explains How He Facilitated Bob Dylan’s Meeting With the Pope Richard Lloyd, Television's Virtuoso Guitarist, Dead at 75 Houston Mayor Limits Cooperation With ICE: ‘Elections Matter’ Good Riddance to the Cybertruck, the Chariot of the Dumbest Gods

Afterwards, Chuwi told Rolling Stone they felt inspired by the mayor’s words. “Being that he’s the mayor of New York, and New York has significant importance in Puerto Rico, it was super important to be able to discuss these matters with him,” says Wester.They also pushed back on critics who might accuse Mayor Mamdani of wading into issues outside his jurisdiction. “My counterargument is that we’re a colony of the United States, and New York is — and has always been — extremely important in Puerto Rico. We’re linked,” says Wester. “The rest of the world is watching what’s happening here on the island, yet our own politicians aren’t addressing it. I think it’s fair game.”

“It’s important to understand that this isn’t like the Financial Oversight Board. Just because people from outside — rather than locals — are addressing these issues, it doesn’t mean they’re coming here to exert control or anything like that,” Adrián says. “People hear ‘the United States is coming here to do things in Puerto Rico’ and immediately think, ‘Oh, Junta de Control Fiscal.’ No, it’s not [necessarily] that. It’s about creating a dialogue between the two sides.”As the meeting wrapped up and Chuwi said their goodbyes, the mayor snuck in one last question: are they doing a show in New York in the near future? Chuwi let Mayor Mamdani know they’ll be seeing each other again soon.

#3393. Resident Evil director Zach Cregger explains why the iPhone is vital to his work

There have been a number of high-profile movies technically shot on iPhone, but in most cases they are using the same professional cinematography kit they would use with other cameras, including lenses costing tens of thousands of dollars.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger uses his own iPhone in a rather different way, taking an approach that could be useful to amateur and professional filmmakers alike …

There’s an ongoing debate about how meaningful it is to claim that a high-profile movie, ad, or keynote video was shot on iPhone. Naysayers argue that the quality is all down to the professional lenses, lighting rigs, and editing employed, while those on the other side of the fence point out that everything was captured by the iPhone sensor.

Cregger mostly sidesteps all of that, describing his own use of an iPhone for shot planning, creating photo boards that accurately represent the image that will be captured by each of the Pro lenses he intends to use.

We grew up with video games informing our visual sense just as much as movies and television did, and I feel like I’m able to make a movie that involves the gameplay. [Here] I have a wide angle lens, our protagonist is in the center of the frame as he’s moving, we’re following locked right behind him when he looks right and we swing, right. His attention is dictating where the camera goes, and I think that the effect of that is is a much more immersive horror experience where you’re feeling informed.

I’m a hyper prepper. I’ve got the iPhone that is, like, always on me. I’ll go to the location with my cinematographer and I’ll use Cadrage, an app that approximates different lenses, and I will basically plan out the sequence. I will know exactly what shot is going to cut to what shot, and I will print out these images and everyone will know we’re using this lens for these shots. This is what’s going to be in the frame, and there’s no guesswork.

He does, however, add that an iPhone is all that you need to make a movie, even if his own budgets give him access to rather more expensive kit.

Anybody can make a movie with what’s in your pocket right now.

At the other end of the scale, I use my iPhone in a similar way to him when planning my own amateur videos. I take still photos to create a photo board so that I have a visual reference for each of my planned shots. The videos themselves may be shot on my Blackmagic rig, my iPhone, or some mix of the two.

You can watch Cregger talk through his process for Apple TV here.

#3392. Richard Lloyd Dies: Guitarist With Influential Punk Pioneers Television Was 75

Richard Lloyd, whose intricate guitar work for the pioneering punk band Television was a fiery counterpart to the sinewy stylings of the band’s co-guitarist and singer Tom Verlaine, died today of the bile duct cancer called cholangiocarcinoma at his home in Chattanooga, Tenn. He was 75.

His death was reported by his family to The New York Times. Lloyd had been diagnosed with the cancer in March.

With his Television bandmates Verlaine, bassist Richard Hell (later replaced by Fred Smith) and drummer Billy Ficca, Lloyd was among the innovative, even revolutionary, New York bands in the mid-1970s to establish the East Village dive bar CBGB as the epicenter of a new downtown music scene. Along with Patti Smith and the Ramones, Television led the way in creating and developing a new sound – defined later (and loosely) as punk – that was often as literate and playful as it was sonically powerful. Related Stories News Paul Howard Dies: Son Of Three Stooges' Moe Howard, Keeper Of The Flame Was 91 News Kimmarie Johnson Dies: 'Beverly Hills, 90210' & 'Dude, Where's My Car?' Actor Was 50

Formed in 1973, Television grew out of the teenage friendship of two Delaware boys, Thomas Miller and Richard Meyers, who by the early ’70s had changed their names to, respectively, Tom Verlaine and Richard Hell and set about developing the spiky guitar sound and keening vocal style (courtesy Verlaine) that would reach its apotheosis in the band’s 1977 masterpiece Marquee Moon. Watch on Deadline

By the time of their 1974 debut at CBGB, Verlaine and Hell had recruited Lloyd to be the group’s second guitarist, a move that gave Television its signature and distinctive dueling Strat-versus-Jazzmaster sound. Unlike the more power-chord-heavy guitar bombast of other bands on the scene, Television specialized in complicated, even byzantine interplay between the six-stringed instruments. And like Patti Smith, Verlaine sang lyrics that signified a devotion to poetry as surely as did his chosen name.

Born Richard John Alt on Oct. 25, 1951, in Pittsburgh, Lloyd grew up in Manhattan’s Greenwich Village and began playing guitar before he hit his teens. He became a regular in the audience of the famed Fillmore East rock palace, mesmerized by the music of The Grateful Dead and other bands of the era. He would be forthcoming about working as a male hustler to support himself during the lean years.

With an early residency at CBGB, Television quickly won over audiences as well as fellow musicians like Patti Smith, Lou Reed and David Bowie, who had caught the band during a trip to New York and set about spreading the word to anyone who would listen. Bowie would later record the group’s song “Kingdom Come” for his 1980 Scary Monsters album

The band’s initial line-up didn’t last long, though, as the old friends Verlaine and Hell began to bicker over everything from their music to the way it was performed on stage. Hell quit in 1975 and formed a sort of punk supergroup called The Heartbreakers with ex-New York Dolls members Johnny Thunders and Jerry Nolan. He eventually left that group to form Richard Hell and the Voidoids.

Hell was replaced in Television by ex-Blondie bassist Fred Smith (not to be confused with Patti Smith’s husband Fred “Sonic” Smith).

Despite its quick success, Television called it quits in 1978, in part because of Lloyd’s increasingly dire heroin addiction and mental health issues. Lloyd would release nine solo albums after Television, and he and Verlaine, despite a prickly relationship, occasionally reunited the band. Neither guitarist would ever match the success or influence of Television in its genre-building heyday.

Lloyd is survived by wife Sheila O’Keefe Lloyd; son Dylan; and brother Eric Lloyd.

#3388. Nintendo Switch games running natively on Apple TV using Claude Code port

A Redditor has just released an open-source project allowing Switch and Switch 2 games to run natively on Apple TV.

So far, both Super Mario Odyssey and Animal Crossing: New Horizons are running, with work ongoing on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom …

We’ve seen people using Claude Code to do some pretty wild things, like reverse engineering Adobe’s pro apps in order to create open-source versions of them. The latest example is a Redditor who’s created an open-source project called TVport to recompile Nintendo games from the Switch and Switch 2 to Apple TV.

Redditor FloatingFalafel shared the work on GitHub. They’ve so far ported three games to Apple TV, with one of them still a work in progress.

I have been working on a fork of nxnative that recompiles your OG Switch and Switch 2 dumps for AppleTV. Currently, this only works on a game-by-game basis. Most games run essentially the same on the switch, but some load textures into memory differently and need to be diagnosed and fixed before the game will run properly. My hope is to find outliers during this beta so more fixes can be added into the program, making it a seamless experience […]

Super Mario Odyssey – Runs at 60FPS, very slight stutters on occasion, and some audio issues around waterfalls specifically.

Animal Crossing: Horizon – Runs at 30FPS, zero issues so far on my plays.

Zelda: TOTK – Still being worked on, runs at 30FPS, gets thermal throttled. I have a work around for the thermal throttle. I have a render scale selection set at 75% and I am working on adding MetalFX upscaling.

They note you’ll need the 4th-gen Apple TV with its 8GB RAM in order to support some games, though these ones run on the 3rd-gen box.

Another Redditor is working on porting Nintendo 64 games to Apple TV using an app called Nativecade. How long any of these types of projects will survive is anyone’s guess.

#3386. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.
