#3343. Phibro Animal (PAHC) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Mineral Nutrition and Performance Products drove growth despite poultry softness.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Phibro Animal Health Corporation (PAHC -6.89%) reported first quarter growth driven primarily by its Mineral Nutrition and Performance Products segments, which offset softer demand in the poultry sector. Management maintained its full-year guidance for fiscal 2027, citing expectations for normalizing poultry demand and the integration of the recently acquired Zoetis medicated feed additive portfolio. The company highlighted a strategic focus on improving cash conversion through inventory reduction and the planned closure of the Chicago Heights manufacturing facility by late 2027.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to Phibro Animal Health Corporation to host webcast and conference call on first quarter results. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Glenn David, Chief Financial Officer. Glenn, please go ahead.

Glenn David: Thank you, Kendra. Good day, and welcome to the Phibro Animal Health Corporation Earnings Call for our fiscal first quarter ending September 30, 2026. My name is Glenn David, and I am the Chief Financial Officer of Phibro Animal Health Corporation. I'm joined on today's call by Dani Bendheim, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Larry Miller, Chief Operating Officer. Also on today's call is Patrick Rodriguez, our Treasurer and new Head of Investor Relations. Welcome, Patrick, to the call, and I'm going to turn things over to you.

Patrick Rodriguez: Thank you, Glenn, and I look forward to interacting with all of you in the coming months. Today, we will cover financial performance for our first quarter and provide financial guidance for our fiscal year ending June 30, 2027. At the conclusion of our remarks, we will open the lines for your questions. I would also like to remind you that we're providing a simultaneous webcast of this call on our website, pahc.com. Also, on the Investors section of our website, you will find copies of the earnings press release and quarterly Form 10-Q as well as the transcript and slides discussed and presented on this call.

Our remarks today will include forward-looking statements, and actual results could differ materially from those projections. For a list and description of certain factors that would cause results to differ, I refer you to the forward-looking statements section in our earnings press release. Our remarks include references to certain financial measures, which were not prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles or U.S. GAAP. I refer you to the non-GAAP financial information section in our earnings press release for a discussion of these measures. Reconciliations of these non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable U.S. GAAP measures are included in the financial tables that accompany the earnings press release.

We present our results on a GAAP basis and on an adjusted basis. Our adjusted results exclude acquisition-related items, unusual nonoperational or nonrecurring items, including stock-based compensation, other income expenses as separately reported in the consolidated statements of operations, including foreign currency, losses, gains net, income taxes related to pretax income adjustments and unusual or nonrecurring income tax items. Now let me introduce our President and Chief Executive Officer, Dani Bendheim, to share his opening remarks. Dani?

Daniel Bendheim: Thanks, Patrick, and good morning, everyone. Patrick, welcome to your first call. Fiscal 2027 is off to a good start. Sales grew 6% to $386.8 million and adjusted EBITDA grew 4% to $64.3 million. And we did that against a tough comparison coming off a very strong first quarter a year ago. Let me spend a few minutes on what drove the quarter and how we're thinking about the rest of the year. Our 2 non-Animal Health segments did a lot of the heavy lifting this quarter. Performance Products grew 16% and Mineral Nutrition grew 17%. I want to spend a moment on Mineral Nutrition because I think it's part of our business that tends to get overlooked.

Part of this quarter's growth reflects higher prices for zinc, copper and other underlying commodities, and those prices obviously move up and down. But over time, we've also been moving this business towards the higher margin, faster-growing parts of the market, including plant nutrition, dairy and pet food. Customers in these markets are asking for more on ingredient sourcing, quality, consistency and technical support. Those requirements play to our strengths because of the investments we've made in talent, facilities and processes. That's a credit to the Mineral Nutrition management team who have been patient in building those relationships and capabilities. We expect the business to continue growing in these higher-margin areas.

In Animal Health, sales grew 3%, about right where we planned. MFAs were up 6% with good demand in North America and Asia and continued growth in ethanol processing aids, and that's net of a $5.2 million decline in Virginiamycin in Brazil. Nutritional specialties and vaccines were each down 2%, mostly on softer poultry purchases in North America and Brazil, plus some timing in Asia. Now people are still buying chicken. The pressure is on the producer side. Based on reports from several large protein companies over the last couple of weeks, U.S. chicken supply was up a little over 2%, which outpaced demand and pushed prices down and producer margins have come off last year's unusually strong levels.

In Brazil, exports have been strong, but the domestic market was soft. The number of birds being raised is a healthy number, and that's ultimately what matters most for us. When margins tighten, customers look harder at every input cost they purchase. A producer counts cost per pound to see what our products return, but some customers trim spending and cut inventory, and we saw a bit of that in our poultry sales this quarter, particularly in nutritional specialties and vaccines. The underlying demand for chicken is there, and we do well when it is. We see this pullback as temporary, and we expect it to normalize over the course of this fiscal year.

Our forecast still has both of these product lines growing in the mid- to high single digits for the year. Animal Health adjusted EBITDA in the quarter was down 1% from last year, though better than we had planned. Part of that reflects costs that moved from the first quarter into the second. On Virginiamycin in Brazil, the transition period ended in October. Our conversations with regulators about therapeutic claims are ongoing. And now that the Brazilian election has passed, we're hopeful we'll see some movement. We haven't built any further Virginiamycin sales in Brazil into this year's numbers. If an approval comes, it's upside.

On the full year, we expect protein demand to continue growing, but producer profitability is likely to phase off in the near term and recent trade and disease disruptions in protein markets add to the pressure. That's reflected in our outlook. So we're keeping our fiscal 2027 guidance where it was. Net sales of $1.5 billion to $1.6 billion, adjusted EBITDA of $258 million to $268 million and adjusted diluted EPS of $3.41 to $3.59. Two other updates. First, the closure of our Chicago Heights plant remains on schedule. Production should wind down in the summer and the early fall of 2027 with those products moving to our other Phibro plants and the contract manufacturers. Second, cash.

We were cash positive in the quarter, but I am not satisfied. We're carrying more inventory than we needed and bringing it down this year is a priority for me and for our whole team. Better cash conversion gives us more flexibility on debt, on investment and on returns to shareholders. So a good quarter with plenty of work still ahead. With that, let me turn the call over to Glenn.

Glenn David: Thanks, Dani. Starting with our Q1 performance on Slide 4. First, net interest expense declined $0.8 million, reflecting lower interest rates and higher interest income, including interest received on our IEEPA tariff recoveries. Second, foreign currency was a $0.4 million gain this quarter compared to a $2 million loss a year ago, a favorable swing of $3.3 million. And third, income tax expense was $0.5 million lower. Taken together, these items more than offset the lower operating income and drove the $3 million improvement in net income for the quarter. After making our standard adjustments to GAAP results, including acquisition-related items, foreign currency losses and certain one-off items, the first quarter adjusted EBITDA increased $2.4 million or 4% versus prior year.

Adjusted net income of $32.4 million increased $2.5 million, primarily due to higher gross profit, lower interest expense and a lower adjusted effective income tax rate, partially offset by higher adjusted SG&A due to higher employee-related costs. Moving to segment level financial performance on Slide 5. The Animal Health segment posted $293 million of net sales for the quarter, an increase of $9.6 million or 3% versus the same quarter prior year.

Within the Animal Health segment, we reported MFAs and other net sales increase of $11.3 million or an increase of 6% due to increased demand for certain of our MFAs in North America and Asia and higher sales of ethanol processing aids, partially offset by a decrease of $5.2 million in Virginiamycin sales in Brazil, attributable to regulatory developments in the country. Nutritional Specialty net sales decreased $1.1 million or 2% due to lower poultry demand in North America and decreased aquaculture demand in South America, partially offset by higher overall demand in China and higher companion animal sales.

Vaccines net sales decreased by $0.6 million or 2% due to lower demand for poultry products in Brazil and lower sales in Asia, partly due to timing, offset by higher swine demand in North America and higher sales of adjuvant products. Animal Health adjusted EBITDA decreased $1 million due to higher SG&A, offsetting higher gross profit from increased sales. Moving on to first quarter financial performance for our other business segments on Slide 6. Starting with Mineral Nutrition. Net sales for the quarter were $73.6 million, an increase of $10.6 million or 17% due to an increase in demand and average selling prices for zinc oxide, copper and trace minerals. Looking at our Performance Products segment.

Net sales of $20.2 million reflects an increase of $2.7 million or 16% as a result of an increase in demand for copper-based and fluoride products. Mineral Nutrition and Performance Products adjusted EBITDA increased $1.6 million and $1.2 million, respectively. Corporate expenses decreased $0.6 million, driven by lower consulting and business development costs. Turning to key capitalization-related metrics on Slide 7. We generated $22 million of positive free cash flow for the 12 months ending September 30, 2026. We generated $86 million of operating cash flow and invested $64 million in capital expenditures. Cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments were $83 million at the end of the quarter.

Our gross leverage ratio was 2.9x at the end of the first quarter based on $740 million of total debt and $257 million of trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA. Our net leverage ratio was 2.6x at the end of the first quarter based on $656 million of net debt and $257 million of trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA. On interest rates, there are no changes to our current swap arrangement. Turning to dividends. Consistent with our history, we paid a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share or $4.9 million in aggregate. Now let's turn to Slide 8, which lays out our guidance for fiscal year 2027.

We are maintaining our previous guidance for fiscal year 2027 as follows: Net sales at $1.550 billion to $1.6 billion. This represents a growth range of 2% to 5% and a midpoint of approximately 4%. Total adjusted EBITDA of $258 million to $268 million. This represents a growth range of 1% to 5% and a midpoint of approximately 3%. Our adjusted effective income tax rate for fiscal year 2027 is estimated at approximately 20% and includes the benefit of the resolution of foreign tax audit expected in the future quarter. We do expect our adjusted effective income tax rate to be higher in fiscal year 2028. Adjusted net income of $140 million to $147 million.

This represents growth of 6% to 11% with a midpoint of approximately 9%. GAAP net income and EPS assumes constant currency and no additional gains or losses from FX movements. As we look ahead to the second quarter, we want to highlight a comparability item. In the second quarter of fiscal year 2026, net sales were reduced by approximately $13 million of product returns related to the transition of certain Tier 3 markets, including Canada and Europe from Zoetis back to Phibro. So as Dani mentioned, we do see squeezed producer margins in both our poultry segments as well as the swine industry. This is a factor of higher supply versus the demand, which has reduced wholesale prices for both chicken meat as well as pork prices.

They've also -- our customers have also experienced higher input costs, certainly with grain, primarily corn, but also in fuel and some of the other inflationary increases that they've seen, and this has caused the pricing pressure there. In the dairy segment, milk prices are hovering at farm gate around $20 per hundredweight. This is about breakeven for many dairy producers. One of the areas that the producers have seen as far as profitability of their farm is the sale of day-old calves, which is still over $1,000 per calf, anywhere from $1,000 to maybe up to $1,500 per calf. So that's a little bit of outlook what we see currently and also into 2027 for incoming feeder cattle supply.

#3342. Report: Apple’s planned $7 billion bond sale attracts four times as much demand

Apple has filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds. Here are the details.

Over the past week, several Big Tech companies have turned to the bond market to raise billions of dollars amid growing investments in AI infrastructure.

Meta, for instance, just raised $15 billion through a US bond offering, followed by another €9 billion (roughly $10 billion) in European bonds. Earlier this week, Alphabet raised €6 billion (approximately $6.7 billion), while Microsoft completed a $25 billion bond sale last week, its first since 2017.

Apple has also turned to bond sales in the past to raise billions of dollars.

Previous offerings include those in 2015, 2019, 2020, and 2021. Most recently, Apple raised $4.5 billion through a four-part bond offering in May 2025, which attracted approximately $10 billion in investor orders.

Earlier today, Apple filed a preliminary prospectus with the SEC outlining plans to issue seven series of bonds maturing between 2028 and 2036.

However, while other Big Tech companies have been borrowing heavily amid growing AI infrastructure investments, Apple’s filing makes no specific mention of AI.

Instead, the company says it intends to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, potentially including stock buybacks, dividends, acquisitions, and debt repayment, as it has done in previous bond offerings.

And while the prospectus didn’t specify how much Apple intends to raise, Bloomberg reported soon after that the company is targeting approximately $7 billion, with investors already placing orders totaling around $31 billion.

According to Bloomberg, strong investor demand has also helped Apple secure more favorable borrowing terms, with investors willing to accept lower interest rates than those offered by Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle in their recent bond sales.

All of this is happening amid a massive tech sell-off, which saw the Nasdaq 100 plunge more than 6% at one point today, with Nvidia shares falling about 8% and the S&P 500 dropping nearly 4%.

Apple’s own stock is also taking a hit, trading down 1.49% at the time of publication, but it is faring better than those of its Big Tech peers, whose stocks have become more closely tied to the AI spending boom.

Be that as it may, Apple is expected to finalize the size and pricing of its bond offering soon, potentially as early as later today, after which the company will file the definitive terms with the SEC.

#3341. IEEE Report Highlights How Members Are Engineering for Public Good

They include humanitarian initiatives and STEM education programs

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

IEEE MOVE, EPICS in IEEE, the IEEE Global Museum, and the TryEngineering Summer Institute, were some of the projects showcased in the 2025 Social Impact Report.

Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.

Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles:

“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”

Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.

“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.

“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

To truly build core strength, you need to target the deep stabilizing muscles that sit beneath more superficial layers like your abs. And to do that, you need to overload them using the correct exercises.

Below, I share three exercises you can try for a stronger, more stable core. These moves target muscles like your obliques, which run down either side of your waist and assist with movements like side bends, and the deep layer of muscle known as the transverse abdominis.

These exercises set your core alight, but they also build strength where it matters: the muscles that support balance, stability and posture. Read on to learn how to do them with proper form.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness | Workout Tips & Gear (@tomsguidefitness)

I recommend 45 seconds on and 15 seconds off for 5 rounds. Here's a little more about the moves you'll be doing. And remember to check out the video above.

If you experience pain, stop immediately and speak with a personal trainer or medical professional for further guidance.

Pallof presses are an anti-rotation exercise, meaning you'll engage your deep stabilizers to prevent turning your body to the side. As you perform them, try to keep your hips square and press your hands away in line with your shoulders.

Move slowly for three seconds out and three seconds in. Ideally, you'd perform this with a reformer, but if you don't have one, you can just as easily tie a resistance band to a non-moving object and use it as an anchor.

Ab roll-outs are fantastic for working your shoulders, arms, abs, the deeper core muscles and hips. You'll feel this down the front of your stomach and along your waist. Unlike using an ab roller, you should feel secure using the reformer bed, and setting the springs means you'll feel challenged during the roll-out and roll-in phases.

As above, I'd use an ab roller if you don't have access to a reformer bed, but make sure your shoulders stay stacked over the roller. Move out slowly, then squeeze your abs and lift your hips to draw the carriage back in. You should aim to create a slight dome through your upper body to help protect your back.

Both feet working together force your transverse abdominis to work harder. Planks target muscles across your entire body, while your hips assist in driving your knees in and your glutes activate to protect your lower back and help stabilize your pelvis.

The slower you move, the harder this becomes. It's completely normal for your hamstrings and quads to burn during this exercise, as well as your arms and shoulders.

Your hip flexors help lift your legs with each rep, but try not to let them take over. If you're feeling the exercise more in your hips than anywhere else, focus on core engagement.

You're looking to maintain a straight spine as you simply draw your knees in, then press your legs away from you. You don't need a reformer bed for this exercise; sliders work well, too.

#3339. iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how

iPhone Duo has only been available for a couple weeks, but Apple keeps improving the product with software enhancements. The latest arrives in the iOS 27.3 beta via a convenient keyboard update.

If you’re one of the fortunate early adopters who managed to get an iPhone Duo on or near launch day, you may have noticed that changes keep arriving via software updates.

iPhone Duo shipped with iOS 27.1, but just a few days later iOS 27.2 arrived and added Apple Pencil support and Edge Light for video calls.

Now just about one week later, the iOS 27.3 beta has introduced even more changes.

Reachability lets you slide outer display content to the left or right to make it more reachable. And as highlighted by Beta Profiles on X, the keyboard has gotten an improvement too.

iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z

The keyboard refresh with narrower keys and smaller font makes it easier than before to type on the iPhone Duo’s outer screen, especially one-handed.

It’s a subtle difference, but one that early testers have found a clear upgrade.

By combining keyboard changes with Reachability, iOS 27.3 offers a noteworthy improvement to the one-handed iPhone Duo experience.

Have you tried the new iPhone Duo keyboard in iOS 27.3? How is it working for you? Let us know in the comments.

J. Crenshaw: Thank you, Andy, and good morning to everyone joining us today. Our third quarter results were in line with our expectations and consistent with the outlook we provided on our call last quarter. Revenue improved 25% sequentially and adjusted EBITDA improved to $1.9 million. Following the conclusion of multiple large contracts at the end of 2025, we have now turned the corner with momentum continuing to build ahead of what we expect will be a record 2027 for Stabilis. The driver of the sequential improvement from the second quarter was the short-term behind-the-meter power generation contract we secured earlier this year to support the commissioning of a U.S. data center. We began delivering LNG under the agreement in August.

As a result, data center-related revenue represented 17% of our total revenue in the third quarter compared to less than 1% in the second quarter. This project will conclude in the fourth quarter. Looking ahead, our focus is squarely on 2027. Our multiyear agreement to supply LNG for behind-the-meter bridge power at a U.S. data center expected to be the largest contract to date in our company's history remains on track to begin in the first quarter of 2027 and will ramp during the second and third quarters. We are also finalizing LNG supply agreements for the project, along with backup supply alternatives to support reliable delivery. We think about these opportunities in 4 phases: construction, commissioning, bridge power and long-term backup. Our commercial team is bidding on additional work across multiple phases of data center demand. We believe we are well positioned to extend our growth runway well beyond 2027 and the contract that begins next year. Outside of the data center market, aerospace remains the other key growth engine of our business.

Revenue from aerospace customers increased 49% year-over-year in the third quarter, driven by the increasing pace of launch and testing activity and a growing number of commercial space customers. These customers have demanding purity and delivery requirements and the operating track record we have built with them is difficult to replicate. We are currently in discussions with multiple space customers for long-term offtake agreements. Turning to Galveston. We continue to engage with prospective customers and financing partners, and we believe the project offers an attractive long-term growth opportunity for Stabilis. That said, we are not ready to commit to a time line for FID, which remains subject to arranging a final financing structure and securing sufficient commercial offtake.

While we remain super excited about the long-term value of the project and what it could and we believe will create, our primary short-term and near-term growth opportunities remain in the aerospace and behind-the-meter data center power projects. To close, the third quarter marked the beginning of a transformational period for Stabilis. While fourth quarter revenues will reflect the conclusion of our short-term data center project, we expect meaningful revenue growth in 2027. We have returned to profitability on a net income basis. Our largest contract is funded and on schedule, and our growth end markets are expanding.

We expect this momentum to build in 2027, and we remain committed to delivering value for our customers and our shareholders through disciplined capital allocation and focused execution. With that, I'll turn the call over to Andy for a detailed review of our financials.

Andrew Puhala: Thank you, Casey. I'll begin with a discussion of our third quarter performance, followed by an update on our cash flow, balance sheet, liquidity and capital spending. Third quarter revenue was $14.8 million, a decrease of 27% compared to the third quarter of 2025. Similar to the first 2 quarters of the year, the year-over-year decline reflects the completion of large marine and power generation contracts in the fourth quarter of 2025, partially offset by continued growth in aerospace, where revenue increased 49% compared to the prior year period as well as growth in our legacy industrial business. On a sequential basis, revenue increased $2.9 million or 25% from $11.9 million in the second quarter.

That increase was primarily driven by the short-term data center contract that began deliveries in August, which took data center-related revenue from less than 1% of the total in the second quarter to 17% in the third. Adjusted EBITDA was $1.9 million in the third quarter compared to $2.9 million in the prior year period, with the decrease attributable to the completion of the 2 large multiyear contracts in the fourth quarter of 2025. Sequentially, adjusted EBITDA increased to $1.9 million from $0.1 million in the second quarter, primarily due to the higher revenues.

Net income was $0.2 million or $0.01 per diluted share compared to net income of $1.1 million in the third quarter of 2025 and a net loss of $4.6 million in the second quarter. I would also note that SG&A was $2.5 million in the quarter, essentially flat with the second quarter and down from $2.8 million a year ago. Turning to cash flow. Operating cash flow was $3.9 million in the third quarter compared to $2.4 million a year ago and included a $5 million customer advance payment for our 2027 data center contract. Second quarter operating cash flow was $7.1 million, which also included a $5 million advance payment.

So the sequential decline primarily reflects changes in working capital. Year-to-date, cash flow from operations totaled $23.4 million, reflecting the full $25 million of advanced payments we've now received under the contract. At quarter end, cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash totaled $18.4 million compared to $18.9 million at the end of the second quarter. Of the $18.4 million, $16.8 million is restricted to support equipment purchases and other preparations for the 2027 data center contract and $1.5 million is unrestricted. Capital expenditures totaled $4 million during the quarter compared to $2.3 million in the second quarter, bringing year-to-date capital spending to $11.5 million. These expenditures were primarily related to equipment and infrastructure for the upcoming data center contract.

Looking ahead, we expect to continue investing to secure equipment and guaranteed supply ahead of the first quarter 2027 start, and we expect those investments to continue to be funded by the advanced payments already received. Before I close, a brief reminder on the points we made last quarter about the earnings profile of the business as we continue to scale. Nothing here is new, and we're not providing 2027 guidance, but with the third quarter now behind us, they're worth keeping in mind. First, our fixed cost base is largely in place, and we do not expect those costs to grow in proportion to revenue as the 2027 contract comes online, which should drive meaningful operating leverage.

Second, we'll service much of the incremental power generation demand with third-party LNG, so it requires limited incremental capital and preserves our plant capacity to support continued growth with our aerospace and other existing customers. The equipment for the 2027 contract is being funded by advanced payments already received. And third, our contracts pass through all commodity price risk. Taken together and in the context of a materially larger revenue base in 2027, this should translate into meaningful growth in adjusted EBITDA dollars and margin expansion into the high-teens as execution accelerates. That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, please open the line for the Q&A session.

J. Crenshaw: Yes. Let me start, Marty. And again, thanks for joining the call today and covering the company. One is the behind-the-meter power business that works in hyperscaler data centers, just distributed power markets, like all types of different end markets. Second is this giant marine bunkering infrastructure opportunity. And finally, it's the aerospace business that we've been heavily involved with since, I guess, 2018, 2019, quite some time.

And we provide high purity, reliable supply to people in the aerospace, primarily related to rockets and launching rockets primarily for telecommunications, satellites, different things of the nature. We don't know exactly everything they do, but mainly those end markets. And we are just seeing the maturing of the business with both additional customers, so more clients that are real clients that buy product and need product and the expansion and increasing the launching and testing by all of those clients.

And so that both expansion of the customer base and maturing of the customer base and the increased activity of all the customers across that industry is driving the growth and our historic performance is leading us to be successful in some of the market. We certainly don't have all of anything, but we have proximity to some clients and historical relationships with others, and we expect it to be a meaningful growth area for us. One of the challenges with the customers is due to the newness of some of the programs, you have anomalies, you have changes in timing, you have regulatory stuff that everybody is going through.

So that changes some of the visibility of cadence of everything, but we're starting to see clients ask for multiyear offtake arrangements, and we're having multiple customers that were involved with that. At the same time, there's conversations out there about some of the clients wanting to vertically integrate. So you have a lot of noise out there, but the growth is kind of beyond any of the negative noise out there. So I touched it from a high, high level, and then I'll let Andy add to it if there's anything to add. But we expect it to continue to grow, to continue to grow as a -- in volume and revenue.

As a percentage of the overall company, when you see the new behind-the-meter activity that's contracted, that may grow -- as you look at percentages, that may just outgrow that growth rate next year, but we're seeing some tremendous growth rate and multiyear contracting happening in the aerospace industry. Your last question was, will we have enough demand or term contracts to add capacity? And we think we hope to and if they want to contract that, we're in some discussions to add infrastructure and capacity. We've talked about contracting with -- even in the Galveston facility to bring it inbound in land from there. We've talked about additional expansion opportunities with infrastructure.

So we're actively involved with that, but we don't have anything to give you any forward guidance on that other than multiple customers now, multiple term contracting negotiations going on. So real positive overall market movement.

Barry Haimes: Congrats on the quarter. I had a couple of questions. Andrew Puhala: Yes, Barry. What we've disclosed publicly is that it's roughly a $200 million contract over 2 years, and it will ramp starting at beginning of next year. Now it's bridge power, so a lot of these bridge power contracts depend on when the data center gets their permanent connection. So the initial contracts for 2 years, I think it is possible that, that gets extended depending on the timing of grid connections and that sort of thing, but we just don't know yet.

Barry Haimes: Got it. Okay. Second question, could you give a little more of an update on the marine market? And do you still have the cruise customer you used to have? And just a little bit more color on that market.

J. Crenshaw: Yes. So I'll take it from a high level and then let Andy come in after that. But the cruise or I should say, marine bunkering business is something we've been doing. We have a specific project that we've talked a lot about in the Houston Ship Channel, specifically Galveston related to a couple of different cruise customer opportunities. We have one contract in hand with a long-term customer relationship.

And when you look at the macro right now and you look at the alternatives of our really strong, high creditworthy cruise customers, they can either use marine gas oil, which is kind of a diesel-based product or LNG and their ships have switching capability. And because of the disruptions globally and the increased cost around those alternatives, there need for a fit-for-purpose asset to make LNG molecules and then have fit-for-purpose delivery capability and bunkering vessel is high. And the macro is better than it's ever been for us to get an asset financed with enough adequate offtake to help that process happen.

And one of the challenges with this offtake agreements to get the project financing is the duration of contracting and how the contracting works to make the project financing work. This project is a $350 million total project, and it requires significant committed offtake over a significant amount of time to make the project financing work for everybody. And so we're just working through those processes, but the macro is really strong on moving that project forward. And Stabilis' project is the furthest along and we believe the most efficiently cost process in the Gulf Coast region. And so we believe we're the leader of the pack in that area, but we still haven't gotten the project to final FID.

Barry Haimes: Okay. Great. And just one quick follow-up on that. Is the -- in terms of how much offtake is committed, I mean, just ballpark it, is it 1/3 committed half, 2/3? Like just where are you in that process? What inning are we in, if you will?

J. Crenshaw: Yes. Well, right now, we've got about 25% of the committed offtake that we -- of that facility, the 350,000 gallons a day production. We don't need 100% offtake, but we need more than what we have now.

Barry Haimes: Got it. Fair enough. And then just last question. And where do you think it's most representative, either the third quarter just reported, year-to-date estimate for '27, what -- I'm not looking for precision. I'm just looking for a ballpark.

J. Crenshaw: Yes. Let me give you the ballpark real quick. I think the best thing to do is to think about '27 and '28 where we have booked and contracted right now. So we've already disclosed that we're assuming -- we have one contract that's a $200 million contract, plus or minus, think about $100 million in revenue a year. We have other behind-the-meter power opportunities that we are bidding and actively working on and intend to execute on. And then you talk about marine, where we really see marine being very strong for Stabilis is out past not next year, but hopefully getting some real revenue and earnings back during 2028. And when you look at the 10 years past there, we're really excited about that being an anchor term duration while we have up and downs from both aerospace and behind-the-meter projects. So that is not perfectly clear explanation, but we see short term, those kind of percentages happening.

And then when you look 3 years out and further and you start talking about how that backup power on behind-the-meter demand starts happening where you need like peaking opportunities with LNG around large behind-the-meter projects, and you continue to see the aerospace growing, those can be major, major long-term contributors consistent. And -- but obviously, once we get the asset in on the -- an FID the marine project, that will be a meaningful percentage of revenue at that point in time. Matthew Dhane: Okay. That is helpful. Matthew Dhane: Understood. I hope you win more than your fair share.

#3336. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

AI slop is a small problem for Wikipedia. The bigger problem is very biased editing on anything with even minimal political implication. And that's a human problem, not AI.
